abstract: The acquisition of rights by an employer in the inventions of his employees is a topic generally apart from the question of giving the employee-inventors rewards for making the inventions in issue. In the United Kingdom and the United States the vesting of the invention in the employer has usually been without reward to the employee-inventor. Likewise, in the case of the ‘shop right’, a licence has usually been royalty free. In Germany on the other hand a special statute governs the reward to be paid to employee-inventors. Reading Mr Adams' contribution one gains the impression that he would not be averse to the introduction of something similar to this country. He has similarly minded supporters among the ranks of professional engineers and patent attorneys. 1 personally prefer the working out of these problems through our common law rather than through the agency of a substantial bureaucracy which is almost certain to develop once a statute of this nature is brought into existence.

articleTitle: Wiring rules are the foundation stones of standard specifications for equipment used in electrical installations
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Early in its history, the IEC considered the possibility of drawing up standard wiring rules on an international basis but it was not until 1967 that the Council of the IEC was requested, and agreed, to set up Technical Committee No. 64 (TC 64) entitled Electrical Installations of Buildings. This delay was a great pity since experience gained during the formulation of the rules covered by TC 64 indicated clearly that wiring rules are the foundation stones of the standard specifications for equipment used in electrical installations. Had these rules been agreed on internationally before the standards for equipment were drawn up, it is certain that the need for compromise would have been considerably reduced. There would also have been far less variations in approaches to what should have been common requirements in the different equipment standards.

abstract: At a recent interest group meeting some thoughts were expressed amongst members concerning the stimulation of interest on papers given before the Institute. During this exchange I made the suggestion that one thing we seemed to lack was the facility for contribution to a paper as a written text, even after the meeting in order to provoke continuing discussion and exchange on the subject of the paper.
